name: Diego Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the grill at the Copper Grill, a steakhouse down by the river that does about three hundred covers on a Friday. I get in at two, check the meat delivery, cut steaks, light the charcoal, and by six I've got twenty tickets hanging over my head. I've had the same station for four years, and I like it that way. Same grill, same tongs, same rhythm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when the whole line is moving together and nobody has to shout. What wears me out is the heat and the doubles in December, when you do fourteen hours and go home smelling like smoke. My partner Nadia drives a city bus, so we're both tired but we're doing all right. We've got more than nine months put away, and I'm a union member, which still means something in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: you can't download a medium-rare steak. Some places will get fancier ordering screens, and the office will save a bit of time on the rota. Kitchens will still need people who can stand the heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, because nothing in my day changes. The owner, Gus, might use some program for the stock sheets, but I never touch those anyway. My pay stays good, and there are ten steakhouses within a bus ride if Gus ever drives me mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my station and keep going to the union meetings on the first Monday of the month. Put the same four hundred a month into savings, like I've done since I was twenty-three. Nadia and I might finally book that week by the lake in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's nice to picture a world where the noise dies down and the grill is still mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Gus might use a program for stock. Would that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, unless he uses it as an excuse to order less and blame the computer when we run out of ribeye on a Saturday. That happened once already with a new supplier app. I told him to call the butcher like a normal person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, a bit, from the lifting and the standing. Rent keeps going up too, though we can cover it. Other than that, I'm one of the lucky ones in this trade.

say: You can't **download** a medium-rare steak, so kitchens will still need real cooks.
Fancier **ordering screens** won't change what actually happens on the grill.
think: I'm **relieved**, because my station, my pay and my routine stay exactly the same.
If the owner ever annoys me, there are **ten steakhouses** within a bus ride.
do: Keep working the **grill station** at the Copper Grill as normal.
Keep saving **four hundred** a month and attending the first-Monday **union meetings**.
feel: **Calm**, with only a small worry about his **back** and the rising rent.
S0.quote: I'd say what I always say: you can't download a medium-rare steak.
fieldNote: He wants **routine** above everything, and this picture gives it to him.
His only run-in with tech so far is a **supplier app** that left the kitchen short of ribeye.
Strong savings, a union card and plenty of nearby kitchens make him feel **secure**.

steps.text: Keep running the grill station at the Copper Grill
Put four hundred a month into savings as usual
Go to the hospitality union meeting every first Monday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office people should be worried, not us. Software can answer the phone and book tables, fine, but it isn't flipping forty steaks with the ticket rail full. I'd say that to anyone at the pub who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it bothers me more than I'd let on. Our front-of-house team is six people, and if the bookings and the ordering go to a tablet, some of them are gone. Lena on reception has two kids, and she's the first one I'd think of. For me the grill is still safe, as long as robots stay slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring it up at the union meeting and push for a rule that nobody gets cut because of a new system without notice and retraining. I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more, five hundred instead of four. I wouldn't touch any of the new apps myself unless Gus made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job feels fine, but I don't like watching people I work with get squeezed out by a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Gus did make you use a new app on the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it, grumbling, the way I used the new fryer timers. I'd probably ask Marta on the pass to show me twice, because I'm slow with that stuff. I just don't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots are slow. What would you watch for to know that's changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the chain steakhouse up the road gets a robot arm on the grill, that's when I start paying attention. Until something like that works on a busy Friday, it's just a video on somebody's phone.

say: The **office jobs** should worry, because software isn't flipping forty steaks at once.
Booking tables by screen is fine, but the **grill** still needs a person.
think: The **front-of-house** team of six could shrink if bookings move to tablets.
His own grill job feels **safe** as long as robots stay slow.
do: Push the union for **notice and retraining** before anyone is cut for a new system.
Raise monthly savings from four hundred to **five hundred**.
Use new apps only if the owner insists, and ask a colleague to **show him**.
feel: **Uneasy** for colleagues like the receptionist, though not much for himself.
S1.quote: Software can answer the phone and book tables, fine, but it isn't flipping forty steaks with the ticket rail full.
fieldNote: His first worry goes to **colleagues**, especially the receptionist with two kids.
He'll use tech only when **forced**, and admits he's slow with it.
His alarm bell is clear: a **robot grill** working at the chain steakhouse nearby.

steps.text: Ask the union branch for a no-cuts-without-notice rule
Raise monthly savings from four hundred to five hundred
Stay on the grill and learn new apps only when required

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say this is exactly why we need strong unions and laws with teeth. If a company can replace a whole kitchen, the public should get something back, not just the owners. I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I've got until about 2031 and then I'm in real trouble. My job is all hands, so the thinking AI doesn't touch me much, but a robot that can work a grill as well as me is the end of my grill station. Three years isn't long when you're slow to change, and I know I'm slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on extras and push savings hard, maybe seven or eight hundred a month, because nine months of money won't last if the trade goes. I'd get on the union's AI committee if they set one up. I'd vote for whoever promises a wage guarantee for workers pushed out by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got money and I'm young, but the one thing I'm good at has a date stamped on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Nadia talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whether her bus job goes first or mine. Driving is thinking and hands together, so I honestly don't know. We'd sit at the kitchen table and do the sums, and Nadia would make me write them down because I hate doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow to change. What would you change first, if you had to pick one thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd look at butchery, because the cutting I do in the afternoon is the part I love. A robot can probably cut too, eventually, but a proper butcher's counter is about talking to people as well. I'd ask around before I'd ever ask a computer.

say: This is why we need **strong unions** and laws with teeth.
If a company replaces a whole kitchen, the **public** should get something back.
think: He has until about **2031**, when robots could take his grill station.
Three years is short for someone who knows he's **slow to change**.
do: Cut extras and push savings to **seven or eight hundred** a month.
Join the union's **AI committee** if one is set up.
Vote for a **wage guarantee** for workers pushed out by machines.
feel: **Anxious**, because the one skill he trusts now has a **date** on it.
S2.quote: A robot that can work a grill as well as me is the end of my grill station.
fieldNote: He understands the **three-year gap** exactly and counts on it.
He's unsure whether his partner's **bus job** or his grill goes first.
Even under pressure, he'd rather ask people than a **computer** about a new trade.

steps.text: Drop eating out and extras to free up money
Push monthly savings up to seven or eight hundred
Volunteer for the union's AI committee
Vote for a wage guarantee for workers replaced by machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing as before, but louder: unions, rules, and the public getting a share. With five years' warning, nobody gets to say they didn't see it coming. I'd say it at work and I'd say it to Gus's face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 means I'd be thirty-five, with time to learn something else, if I can make myself do it. My problem has never been money, it's that I hate starting over. The extra years help, but only if I actually use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Vito, the butcher on Mill Street, about a Saturday apprenticeship, because cutting meat is the bit I love. I'd still put six hundred a month away. And I'd keep pushing the union for a fund to retrain kitchen workers, paid by the companies that buy the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a softer anxious. Five years feels like enough time to waste if I'm not careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you from going to see Vito?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, probably. I'm good on the grill, and in a butcher's shop I'd be the new guy again, getting told how to hold a knife. Nadia would push me, though. She'd book the meeting and tell me afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the Copper Grill would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young lads on prep, the ones who are nineteen and only know this. I've got savings and a trade certificate. They've got a phone and a bus pass.

say: With **five years' warning**, nobody can claim they didn't see it coming.
Companies buying robots should pay into a **retraining fund** for kitchen workers.
think: Robots by **2034** leave him time to learn something new, if he pushes himself.
His problem isn't money but hating to **start over**.
do: Ask the Mill Street butcher about a **Saturday apprenticeship**.
Lobby the union for a **retraining fund** paid by companies.
feel: **Anxious**, but softer, with a worry that he'll **waste** the extra time.
S3.quote: My problem has never been money, it's that I hate starting over.
fieldNote: **Pride** about being good on the grill is his main brake on change.
His partner is the one who would **book the meeting** for him.
He worries most about the **nineteen-year-old** prep cooks with no savings.

steps.text: Ask Vito at the Mill Street butcher about Saturday apprentice shifts
Save six hundred a month toward a training gap
Push the union for a company-paid kitchen retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for governments to get it right, so there's no excuse. I'd keep saying the same thing about unions and a fair share. People would roll their eyes, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, with robots around 2039 I'd be forty, and I'd probably just keep grilling and tell myself I'll deal with it later. That's my honest weakness. A decade feels like forever when you're standing over charcoal every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and my savings going, maybe four hundred a month like now. I'd vote and sign petitions. I'd watch what happens to the other kitchens first before I change anything myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough away that I'd sleep fine, but I know that's not the same as being ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You just said you'd deal with it later. In the earlier picture you'd go and see the butcher. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. With five years I'd feel pushed, with ten I'd let it slide. That's me being honest about how I work, not how I should work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act sooner in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it with my own eyes. If a robot grill showed up at a place I know, I'd move. Nadia says that's too late, and she might be right.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time** for governments to get it right.
He'd keep pushing for **unions** and a fair share, even if people roll their eyes.
think: With robots around **2039**, he'd probably keep grilling and put it off.
A decade feels like **forever** when you're working charcoal every night.
do: Keep his **grill job** and his usual savings of four hundred a month.
Vote and **sign petitions** for worker protections.
Watch **other kitchens** before changing anything himself.
feel: **Uneasy**, sleeping fine but aware he isn't really **ready**.
S4.quote: A decade feels like forever when you're standing over charcoal every night.
fieldNote: He openly admits that **more time** makes him act less.
He needs to **see a robot** working in a kitchen he knows before he'll move.
His partner thinks waiting is **too late**, and he half agrees.

steps.text: Watch nearby kitchens for robot grills before acting
Sign petitions for protections for replaced workers
Keep grilling at the Copper Grill and saving four hundred monthly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Three years from thinking AI to robots on the grill is too fast for someone like me. What would help is a real retraining wage, paid while you learn, and the union having a seat at the table when the robots come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked who gets the money when the robots work. If the Copper Grill runs with two people instead of twelve, somebody's getting rich, and it isn't going to be the cooks. That's what makes me angry, more than the machines.

headlineQuote: If the Copper Grill runs with two people instead of twelve, somebody's getting rich, and it isn't going to be the cooks.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old grill cook** at a busy riverside steakhouse, four years on the same station.
He has **nine months saved**, a union card, and a partner who drives a city bus.
He loves **routine**, never uses AI tools, and admits he hates starting over.
He's calm in the mild pictures, but **anxious** when robots could reach the grill within five years.
With ten years' warning he'd likely **put off** acting until he sees a robot grill himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years from thinking AI to robots is too fast for him.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining wage** paid while he learns a new trade.
The **union** having a seat at the table when robots come into kitchens.
